title: The Soviet Counterstroke
subtitle: Yelnya: a missed encirclement and a costly Soviet success
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: The 24th Army missed its deadline for trapping the German force at Yelnya. Its continued attacks secured a withdrawal, revealing both Soviet tactical learning and the limits of the victory.
body:
The deadline and the ground still to be taken

The deadline arrived before the victory. By 3 September 1941, the Soviet 24th Army was supposed to have enclosed the German troops at Yelnya and prepared to advance towards Pochinok. Its order of 26 August had set the attack for 30 August. Four days later, German troops still held the salient and its western exit. Soviet pressure would compel them to withdraw, but the outcome would differ from the promised encirclement. The gap between order and result is the central problem of this battle: an army could recover ground without destroying the force it had fought to trap. [1]

A salient is a projection of the front into an opponent’s territory. It offers the army occupying it a forward position, but it also exposes that army to attacks from several directions. At Yelnya, southeast of Smolensk, German forces held an eastward bulge whose communications ran through its western base. Soviet troops could attack the northern and southern shoulders while other formations fixed the defenders along the outward-facing arc. The attraction of the scheme was clear: a relatively short advance across the neck might trap forces occupying a much larger perimeter. Its difficulty was equally important. The two Soviet groups had to progress together, preserve their own flanks and hold the roads they reached against counterattacks.

The fighting grew out of the protracted struggle described in the atlas’s earlier Smolensk studies, not a sudden discovery that the Red Army could counterattack. Soviet forces had been attacking in this area through July and August. German armoured formations had helped create the forward position, but infantry increasingly bore the burden of holding it as mobile forces were assigned elsewhere. General Georgy Zhukov commanded the Soviet Reserve Front, an army-group-level formation; Major General Konstantin Rakutin commanded its 24th Army. Opposite them, German XX Army Corps under Friedrich Materna belonged to Field Marshal Günther von Kluge’s 4th Army. The contest joined Soviet efforts to recover the initiative to Germany’s effort to economise in the centre while conducting major operations on its wings.[2][3]

That relationship gives the chapter its connection with The Southward Offensive. Forces committed to holding Yelnya could not simultaneously reinforce Guderian’s movement into Ukraine. Yet it would be misleading to treat every Soviet attack in the centre as an operation that directly stopped the southern advance. Local pressure could consume German reserves without interrupting a distant spearhead. Yelnya’s significance has to be measured at both levels: what the 24th Army accomplished around the salient and what that achievement did, or failed to do, to the wider German campaign.

A pincer assembled from uneven formations

Rakutin’s northern group included the 102nd Tank Division and the 107th and 100th Rifle Divisions. The southern effort involved the 106th motorised formation and the 303rd Rifle Division, while other units pressed the eastern face. These designations require some caution. A formation called a tank division did not necessarily possess the armoured strength implied by its title after the losses and reorganisations of the summer. Nor did inclusion in an attack order mean that every regiment would move at the same time. The operational reports distinguish sectors, attachments and reserves because an army’s available force was distributed among several immediate tasks.[3]

The orders for Major General Ivan Russiyanov’s 100th Rifle Division show what the northern attack required in practice. Two regiments were to move from the Uzha and the southwestern edge of Mitino towards Bogadilovo and Ageyevka, then continue to further objectives. A third was to advance from the area of Perganovo, seize road junctions and work towards the railway approaches northwest of Yelnya. Additional heavy artillery was attached to support the operation. The division was thus not being directed straight at the town centre. Its task was to work across the northern side of the salient, dislocate the defensive positions there and help close the western exit.[1]

These directions can be read as a chain of practical requirements. Crossing a stream or reaching the edge of a wood would provide a starting position for attacking the next defended locality. Capturing a village would matter because its roads, buildings and surrounding heights could support another stage. Heavy artillery had to suppress positions that riflemen could not bypass safely; infantry then had to occupy the ground before the defenders recovered. If the infantry stopped, the guns could continue expending ammunition without producing a usable passage. If tanks advanced without nearby riflemen, the force that appeared to have broken through could become isolated from the troops needed to secure its gains.

German defence exploited precisely these separations. Soviet reports identify fire from woods, village edges and elevated ground, including mortar fire directed across the line of advance. The infantry divisions holding the salient did not need to defeat the entire Soviet army in a single counterstroke. They needed to prevent separate penetrations from becoming a continuous breach. Maintaining a strong point beside an advancing Soviet regiment could threaten its flank, interrupt its communications and force it to divert troops. The value of these positions was therefore greater than their size on a map. A grove or a handful of houses could delay a movement intended to close an army-scale encirclement.[1]

The first attacks and the limits of firepower

The offensive opened on the morning of 30 August with artillery preparation. Its immediate results were uneven. The 100th Division’s report at 13.00 describes stubborn German fire from the woods south of Bogadilovo, from Ageyevka and from neighbouring heights. Its 85th Rifle Regiment was in woodland east of Guryevo; battalions of the 355th remained around Mitino and the stream southwest of it. The 331st was still distributed around Bykhovo and the Uzhitsa. These positions were well short of the day’s intended objectives. Russiyanov responded by ordering regrouping, closer contact between the 355th and 85th Regiments and renewed efforts against the mill at Bogadilovo.[1]

Russiyanov’s response identified a coordination failure. Neighbouring regiments had to establish contact before either could safely exploit a gain. Otherwise, a battalion advancing past a wood might expose itself to fire from a position its neighbour was expected to suppress. The order therefore addressed where units should meet and the flank from which they should attack. Determination alone could not supply this information. Repeating the assault without changing the relationship between the regiments risked repeating the loss.

The next day’s army account, reproduced in David Glantz’s documentary reconstruction, describes similar difficulty in the 102nd formation. A battalion that had reached a grove became separated from neighbouring troops and withdrew under fire. The report connected the failure to the absence of even a company in reserve to exploit the initial advance. It also recorded that personnel had been detached to form a special group under Colonel Ivan Matveyevich Ivanov. This is a concrete example of the cost of concentrating force: a detachment intended to make the decisive breakthrough could weaken the formations expected to create the opportunity for it.[3]

Ivanov’s group was conceived as a force for the enemy’s rear communications, combining tanks, motorised infantry and supporting guns. Its orders sought a movement beyond the immediate defensive belt towards roads west of Yelnya. The conception was more sophisticated than an undifferentiated frontal assault, but its employment depended upon the main attacking formations making sufficient progress. A mobile group cannot exploit an opening that does not yet exist. Holding it ready preserved a possible means of turning local success into encirclement; feeding it into the initial struggle risked consuming that capability before it reached the roads whose seizure justified its formation.[3]

The artillery problem was equally material. Zhukov’s criticism of the army’s gun maintenance and employment concerned the difference between possessing weapons and obtaining effective fire from them. At Yelnya, the target was often a defended locality whose occupants could survive a preparation and reappear when Soviet infantry advanced. Accurate reconnaissance and the timing of supporting fire mattered alongside the quantity of ammunition. A bombardment that failed to suppress the relevant position could impose a logistical cost without removing the tactical obstacle. Repeated attacks then demanded more shells, more movement by supply vehicles and more effort from gun crews already engaged in a sustained battle.[3]

What headquarters knew by 3 September

On 1 September, Zhukov told Stalin’s secretary Aleksandr Poskrebyshev that the enemy at Yelnya should be encircled within two days. The same conversation recorded a serious reverse on the Reserve Front’s Roslavl axis, where the 211th Rifle Division had retreated and endangered a neighbouring formation. Zhukov asked to postpone a journey to Moscow so that he could intervene at the front, and Stalin agreed. The exchange reveals the extent of the front commander’s responsibilities. Success around Yelnya was being pursued while another part of his command required immediate attention. It also places a contemporary prediction beside its eventual outcome: confidence in an imminent ring was not evidence that the ring already existed.[3]

The 24th Army’s summary for 2 September gives a less expansive picture. Elements of the 100th Division remained near Sadki, Guryevo and Mitino. Some positions were described in hundreds of metres from a village or wood rather than in the larger distances imagined by the original order. The summary also stated that information about losses and captured material had not yet arrived. That absence matters when reading later claims of decisive success. Headquarters could know that troops had moved to a particular line while still lacking a reliable account of what the movement had cost or what it had done to the enemy.[1]

The northern attack was nevertheless approaching ground that threatened the German exit. On 3 September the struggle continued around the approaches to Nezhoda and the railway northwest of Yelnya. The army sought to push the northern and southern groups towards one another, but the connecting corridor remained open. Descriptions of a neck only several kilometres wide convey the danger more accurately than descriptions of a completed pocket. A narrow passage could still carry men, guns and vehicles if its shoulders remained defended and the movement was organised. The operational question was whether the Soviets could close and hold it before the Germans withdrew.[3]

A commander lost during the attack

Accounts collected in Glantz’s study connect Colonel Ivanov’s death with the fighting on 3 September. Veteran E. Grigoryev recalled that Ivanov was wounded and placed in a truck, which was then struck as it left the fighting area. Army signals officer Nikolai Yarantsev remembered reporting the death to Rakutin, who had recently spoken with Ivanov and initially struggled to accept the news. These are retrospective recollections, and they should not be mistaken for a minute-by-minute medical record. They nevertheless show how abruptly an operation could lose the officer around whom a temporary group had been organised. Ivanov’s detachment was not merely a collection of weapons: its purpose depended upon communication between units drawn from several formations. The death of its commander imposed an organisational loss as well as a personal one.[3]

A further reinforcement order was issued at 23.00 on 3 September. Colonel Andrei Akimenko’s 127th Rifle Division was to send its 395th Rifle Regiment into the operational control of the 102nd Tank Division. The order named two marching columns and their routes towards Novobrykino and Praslovo. It directed that all available vehicles of the divisional transport company be assembled for a combined movement. At the same time, a battalion of the 535th Regiment was to take over the departing regiment’s defensive sector. The reinforcement therefore required transport, a handover and a temporary redistribution of risk elsewhere along the front.[1]

The follow-up report dated 4 September confirms that the 395th Regiment began moving at 00.30 and that the replacement battalion occupied its former sector later that morning. It does not establish that the regiment had already completed every subsequent combat task. This pairing of an order and a report is unusually valuable: it shows a proposed movement becoming an actual departure. It also corrects the impression that all the forces credited with the eventual victory were already in their final positions on 30 August. The army continued assembling the means of attack while the battle was underway.[1]

The force behind the regimental names

The 127th Division’s earlier returns explain why this redistribution was demanding. On 15 August, its staff reported severe shortages of personnel and equipment after the Smolensk fighting. One howitzer regiment had only a handful of guns, some unserviceable, and no artillery ammunition. The signals battalion had men but lacked its technical equipment. The division’s report explicitly concluded that its existing condition was insufficient to guarantee the defence of its assigned sector. These were conditions reported more than two weeks before the reinforcement order, not a precise inventory for 3 September. They establish the process of reconstruction from which the regiment was being drawn.[1]

The same return listed horses as well as guns in the light artillery regiment. That detail helps restore the physical character of the Red Army’s work. Moving artillery required teams, harness, fodder and personnel able to handle animals, alongside whatever mechanical transport remained. A regiment could receive a new task faster than its transport could complete it. The 3 September order’s call for available supply vehicles shows one response: use the army’s transport flexibly to accelerate a movement. Such flexibility had limits. A vehicle assigned to carry infantry was temporarily unavailable for its ordinary supply work, and the order’s emphasis on availability should not be mistaken for evidence of an unlimited pool.[1]

Defensive engineering continued alongside preparations for attack. The 127th Division’s August instructions called for protected communications centres, shelters, firing positions and improved observation. Its reconnaissance order of 25 August demanded regular information from neighbouring formations and particular attention to the junction between the 20th and 24th Armies. This was the less conspicuous work that allowed units to be transferred without leaving an entire flank unexamined. It also shows the interaction between material construction and information: a trench could protect its occupants, but it could not warn them that the enemy was assembling beyond an adjacent unit’s frontage.[1]

The engineering instructions, dated by the documentary editors to no later than 12 August, also prescribed the labour that such protection required. Soldiers and commanders assigned to defensive construction were to work fifteen to sixteen hours a day, principally at night. Daytime groups were limited to ten men in places concealed from aerial observation; work completed overnight was to be camouflaged by dawn. These were instructions, not a verified return of hours actually worked. They nevertheless show how the command demanded prolonged physical labour to sustain a defensive position even while it sought opportunities to attack. Darkness offered concealment, but exploiting it reduced the time available for rest. [1]

The same documents reveal the limits of the operational record as a history of the surrounding population. Villages, mills and fields appear as objectives, observation points or routes. The reports establish fighting over inhabited places, but they rarely tell us where residents went, what they could salvage or who survived. It would be unsafe to supply those missing experiences from a generic picture of devastation. What the record does show is that repeated attacks and renewed defensive work kept these localities within an active battlefield. Recovering a village could alter military control without ending the danger around it.

The earlier battle remembered

Konstantin Simonov’s published diary places his first encounter with the Yelnya fighting in July, not September. He later revisited the names of two scouts whom he had described in a wartime newspaper article, explaining that their surnames had been misprinted. Correspondence eventually established their survival. One, Leonid Grishanov, became a teacher after a grave wartime wound; the other, Vasily Palazhenko, continued through the war as an officer. The episode is a reminder that the soldiers of the final offensive carried earlier experiences into it, while the written record itself could distort even a man’s name. Simonov’s retrospective additions should be distinguished from his original observations. They preserve the work of recovering individual lives from an account initially written under the pressures of a retreat and published before anyone could know who would survive.[4]

The wider demands on Soviet endurance

The contemporary diplomatic record places the fighting in a larger setting. On 3 September, while Rakutin’s troops were still attacking, Stalin wrote to Winston Churchill that the Soviet position had deteriorated in Ukraine and around Leningrad. He welcomed additional British aircraft but argued that deliveries arriving in successive small groups could not change the immediate balance by themselves. His request for another front in Europe accompanied demands for continuing material assistance. The message was intended to influence an ally, and its account of danger served that purpose. Nevertheless, its urgency is incompatible with a retrospective narrative in which an approaching success at Yelnya had already solved the Red Army’s strategic difficulties.[5]

Stalin’s demand concerned scale as well as speed. Successive small deliveries could be absorbed into the continuing losses without changing the immediate balance at a threatened front. This was an argument made to secure greater assistance, rather than an independent measurement of everything British deliveries had achieved. It also shows why Yelnya could not stand for Soviet recovery as a whole. The state was simultaneously seeking weapons abroad, moving regiments between sectors and trying to hold cities whose supply routes were under attack. A local offensive had to compete within that larger emergency.

Churchill’s reply of 4 September emphasised the practical obstacles to an immediate landing in western Europe and the supplies Britain could provide. The exchange exposed different strategic time horizons. Moscow needed pressure relieved during a campaign already threatening major population and industrial centres; London argued from the forces and transport available for operations it could actually sustain. These were disagreements within an emerging coalition against Germany, not evidence that either government possessed an effortless solution it merely refused to use. At Yelnya, the result remained dependent on the Soviet soldiers, ammunition and reserves already assembled or close enough to arrive.[5]

Withdrawal and the limits of victory

The German decision to leave the salient developed before its evacuation was complete. Franz Halder’s record of the command conference on 2 September described agreement that the Yelnya bulge should be abandoned, alongside concern about losses and the scarcity of reserves in Army Group Centre. The subsequent withdrawal was conducted in stages, with rear services and supplies moving before the last combat formations. This sequence helps explain how the Germans could lose a forward position without losing all the troops defending it. The army was giving up ground to shorten the front and preserve forces whose continued exposure had become increasingly expensive.[3]

Soviet reporting on 5 September recognised that the character of the battle had changed. The army’s summary distinguished resistance on the flanks from withdrawal in the centre and reported pursuit beginning that afternoon. The 100th Division’s regiments were moving beyond positions that had delayed them for days. By the following evening, the army reported the enemy withdrawing westward and apparently preparing another defensive line along the Ustrom and Stryana. Yelnya itself was retaken on 6 September. The original objective of enclosing and capturing the entire grouping had not been achieved, even though the offensive had forced the abandonment of the salient.[1][6]

Zhukov’s report of 8 September acknowledged that the encirclement had not been completed and connected the failure to insufficient forces, especially tanks on the attacking flanks. That admission is more useful than either a triumphalist description of total destruction or a dismissal of the offensive as meaningless. German withdrawal was a Soviet operational success, limited by the escape of most of the defending formations. The Germans relinquished an exposed position they had defended at considerable cost. They also preserved troops who could fight again on a shorter line. The failed encirclement therefore mattered as much as the recovered town when assessing the result. [6]

Loss figures further qualify the result. Glantz cites the Soviet statistical series as recording 31,853 casualties for the Yelnya operation from 30 August to 8 September: 10,701 irrecoverable losses and 21,152 medical losses. The first category includes men killed, missing and captured; it is not simply a count of deaths. These totals also cannot be compared directly with Soviet wartime claims for German losses accumulated over a differently defined period. The relevant conclusion is that the local victory consumed a substantial part of the force committed to it. Restoring the army’s ability to attack again required replacements, equipment and time, rather than merely a new objective on its map.[7]

The Guards designation followed later. The 100th and 127th Rifle Divisions became the 1st and 2nd Guards Rifle Divisions under the order of 18 September. Their new titles must not be projected back onto the fighting of 3 September. Recognition expressed the importance attached to exemplary formations, but it did not erase their shortages or make their earlier performance uniformly successful. The documentary sequence shows units receiving criticism, rebuilding, undertaking difficult movements and then gaining distinction. That is a more convincing account of military learning than one in which an elite identity existed fully formed before the experience that helped create it.[1]

Yelnya demonstrated that German infantry could be forced off ground it had defended and that Soviet formations could sustain the pressure needed to obtain that result. The missing encirclement exposed what they could not yet reliably do: coordinate converging attacks quickly enough to close the enemy’s exit. The achievement and the limitation belonged to the same battle. As troops occupied the abandoned salient, other Soviet forces faced a new emergency in the north. Leningrad Cut Off follows the loss of the city’s land connection and the effort to keep its inhabitants supplied.
